doc.title: Eddie Metz Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, October 3, 2015

title: Disney years, the Black Dogs and New York
summary: Fifteen years at Disney, jazz parties, the Black Dogs Dixieland band, Steely Dan musings and what staying in New York might have meant.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: Yeah. The bean counters. This is wasted time. Make them fold shirts or something. And they did. They had a couple of managers do that. So I survived Disney for 15 years doing all kinds of different jobs and also working on the outside. And my last few years there was when I really started doing jazz parties and festivals, either as a solo, just a drummer that they invite to the jazz party, or I was working with a band called the Black Dogs which is a great, great Dixieland band. Best band I ever worked with. It was unbelievable. Kind of obscure, and nobody really knew about it other than the people in California at the festivals we played. And we had people lined up around the block. We sold 1,200 cassettes in three days there one time. Playing three sets a day. We couldn’t hand them out fast enough. It was amazing. So that was a hugely powerful band, and then the band leader stole all the money and then disbanded. But, you know, there’s all kinds of stories like that in the music business. Somebody gets greedy. And it really could’ve gone on, because it was so different, it could have gone on to be like a warm-up act for major rock bands, because it was so different. Like Steely Dan — love Steely Dan — I love that band — you never know who’s going to play warm-up for them. Last time I saw them they had an organ trio from Chicago. And they were just great. Guys you never even heard of. Because Donald Fagan heard them playing in a bar somewhere in Chicago. And their drummer, Keith Carlock, you know, he’s huge now. He heard him playing in a bar in New York. Because they actually went to see the guitar player.

And he was playing drums with them. He was just a country boy from Mississippi. James Taylor, Steely Dan, Eric Clapton, he’s doing all these gigs. He’s like Steve Gadd’s sub. What a position that is to be in. And maybe if I’d stuck around New York I could have done more stuff like that or I could be on Broadway. A lot of my friends, John Allred, the greatest trombone player I know, is in New York playing on Broadway, sitting in the pit. Making good money. Making good pension. Not having to be on the road. That’s a
blessing these days, not having to deal with airports and airlines and stuff. I’m not sick of it yet.
